antecedent_conditions: Complex building B with low spatial legibility (deep spatial graph, few landmarks, ambiguous circulation). Person P navigates B under two conditions: A₁ (urgent goal: find specific room quickly) and A₂ (exploratory: discover the building at leisure).
predicted_outcome:
- Under A₁ (urgency): low legibility → high negative PE → frustration, anxiety, negative evaluation. The complexity that produces PE under urgency is the *wayfinding-relevant* complexity (circulation legibility, signage clarity).
- Under A₂ (exploration): low legibility → high positive PE → curiosity, engagement, positive evaluation. The complexity that produces PE under exploration is the *experiential* complexity (spatial discovery, architectural richness).
- Same physical space, same complexity level, opposite affective valence — driven by activity-frame-dependent PE interpretation.
expected_effect_sizes:
- Evaluation difference (same space, different frames): d ≈ 0.7–1.0
- Wayfinding efficiency: A₁ > A₂ (urgency produces more focused search, despite frustration): d ≈ 0.3–0.5
- Anxiety measures (SCR, HR): A₁ >> A₂: d ≈ 0.5–0.8
architectural_consequence: Wayfinding systems must be designed for the highest-urgency expected activity frame. If a space will be used by people in urgent search (hospitals, airports, emergency exits), legibility at the wayfinding level must be maximized regardless of whether this reduces experiential complexity. The two types of complexity can be partially orthogonalized: a building can have high experiential complexity (rich architectural vocabulary) with high wayfinding legibility (clear circulation hierarchy, prominent landmarks, effective signage).
overlap_analysis: Strong overlap with Spatial Navigation (SN) Tier 1 features and Spatial Config (SC) Tier 2 templates (e.g., isovist legibility vs. mystery).
name: Wayfinding Under Different Goal States
